content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem carefully — I shouldn't restate the cost or impact figures as if I calculated them myself, and shouldn't invent my own numbers either, since those were given, not derived. The error rate remains unknown, and the duration should be treated as a lower bound rather than a precise figure.

Root cause here is genuinely unconfirmed at only moderate confidence, so I should present it honestly as a correlation rather than a certainty: a production change to the affected service landed the same minute as onset, and latency climbed immediately while memory stayed flat, pointing toward a bad configuration value — but since there's no diff on record, a code regression or upstream slowdown can't be ruled out, and rollback wasn't possible since no prior revision existed. I'll avoid naming components where possible, referring instead to "the affected service," and flag key assumptions like completeness of log coverage and that the change caused the incident.

For the executive summary I want to state the onset time factually (shortly before 09:00 UTC) since that's given, but explicitly note the total duration and number of affected requests are unknown since the service hadn't recovered as of the last data point. I should also flag that the 08:59 UTC onset time itself is an estimate drawn from an already-elevated four-minute metrics window, so the true onset could be earlier.

Other assumptions worth noting: I classified the deploy as a configuration change purely from its repository path without reading the actual revision contents; the log channel only returned six lines from 08:59–09:02 even after widening the window back to 07:30, which I'm treating as complete rather than truncated; no upstream dependency was ever named in the evidence, so I can neither confirm nor rule out a dependency slowdown; error rate metrics were unreadable so user impact is only inferred from timeout log lines rather than directly measured; and the time the incident sat with the automated responder reflects response duration, not the actual outage length.

assumptions: Onset was placed at 08:59 UTC from a four-minute metrics window that was already elevated at its opening minute; the true onset may be earlier.

The change at the onset minute was treated as a configuration change purely because of its source repository path (k8s-configs, apps/io-shop/production). The revision's actual contents were never read, so 'configuration rather than code' is inferred, not verified.
Causation between that change and the latency is inferred from timing coincidence alone. Correlation at the same minute is the only supporting evidence.

The log channel returned the same six lines whether queried over 33 or 92 minutes, with nothing before 08:59Z. This was assumed to be a complete record rather than a truncated or partially failing log source.
No downstream or upstream dependency is named anywhere in the retrieved evidence, so a dependency slowdown was neither confirmed nor ruled out.
Feature flags were checked and showed no recent changes; this was taken at face value from the flag provider's history.
The service is assumed to have remained impaired after the last minute of metrics read; no recovery signal was observed either way.
Impact on users is inferred from timeout log lines, since the error-rate metric for the incident could not be read.
The interval during which the automated responder held the incident describes how quickly it responded, not how long the service was broken, and is not used here as a duration of impact.
input.executive_summary: Shortly before 09:00 UTC on 24 September 2026, one of our online services began responding slowly. Response times climbed steadily over the following minutes until requests started failing outright on timeout, meaning some customer requests to that service would have been slow and then unsuccessful. Automated monitoring raised an alert and an automated responder took the incident up within about a minute, gathered the service's recent metrics, logs and change history, and concluded that a change pushed to production at the moment the slowdown began was the most likely trigger. It tried to undo that change, but the platform had no earlier version of the service's settings on record to return to, so the undo could not be performed and the incident was handed to humans. The service had still not recovered at the point the available data ends, so how long the disruption lasted and how many requests were affected are not known from this record — only that it was ongoing when the record stops. No reliable error-rate figures could be read for the affected period.
input.root_cause: Not established. The strongest available correlation is a production change to io-shop recorded at exactly the onset minute (08:59:00Z), sourced from the k8s-configs repository at apps/io-shop/production, after which p95 latency rose from a ~220ms baseline through 1800ms to 5000ms client timeouts while memory stayed flat and traffic was flat or declining — a pattern consistent with a configuration value (endpoint, timeout, limit or pool size) being changed into a broken one. The change record carries no diff, so a code regression in the same revision, or a slowdown in an unnamed downstream dependency, remains possible; the revision contents (9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e) and pre-08:59 upstream health signals were never retrieved. The attempted mitigation (rolling the service's configuration back) could not run at all: the platform reported no revision earlier than the one running, so there was nothing to roll back to, and the incident was escalated.
